confidence_note: Book text read. The old 'write an angry letter and sleep on it' premise is NOT in the book and was dropped; story is rebuilt on the book's own anger images and walking practice.
facts: When angry we want to think about the person: his rudeness, dishonesty, cruelty. The more we think about him, listen to him or look at him, the more the anger flares.
'Like a fireman, we have to pour water on the blaze first and not waste time looking for the one who set the house on fire.'

Verse: 'Breathing in, I know that I am angry. Breathing out, I know that I must put all my energy into caring for my anger.' Avoid thinking about the other person and refrain from doing or saying anything while anger persists; that avoids damage we may regret later.
Mindfulness is not a judge but like an older sister comforting her younger sister; awareness does not suppress or drive out anger, it looks after it.

Pillow-pounding: expressing anger may rehearse it and strengthen it. Punching a pillow can work temporarily because the energy is spent and we feel better, but the roots remain; if the seeds are watered again, anger is reborn and we pound again.

Walking meditation when angry: go outside to fresh air, green trees; verse 'Breathing in, I know that anger is here... I know this feeling will pass... I am strong enough to take care of this anger'; give attention to soles and earth; wait until calm enough to look directly at the anger.
After a while the anger subsides, we feel stronger, and then we can observe it and try to understand it.
scene_details: A fireman pouring water on the blaze before looking for who set the fire
A pillow punched in a locked room
Walking outside among trees with the verse, soles on the earth
tension: The urge to go after the person who angered you is exactly what keeps the anger burning.
opening_idea: A fireman who pours water on the blaze before looking for the person who lit it.

lessons.idea: Turn attention to the anger itself first, and hold off on speech and action while it lasts.
lessons.anchor: The fireman image and the pillow that has to be pounded again

reflect_final: The next time you are angry, what could you do with your body in the first ten minutes before you say anything to the person?

use_cases.situation: An annoying message arrives and you want to answer at once
use_cases.move: Leave the reply unsent, go outside and walk with the book's verse, then decide.

use_cases.situation: A partner says something that stings during dinner
use_cases.move: Say you need a few minutes, breathe, and come back when you are calm enough to look at the anger.

use_cases.situation: A colleague takes credit in a meeting
use_cases.move: Stay with your breathing and hold off on any reply until you can name what the anger is about.

pocket_idea: Water the blaze first; the person who lit it can wait until you are calm.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Thinking about the culprit is what feeds the fire.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Hanh: fireman, blaze first. Pillow-pounding only tires the anger. Walk, breathe, wait, then look.
